source.title: Language Models Resist Alignment: Evidence From Data Compression
source.authors: Jia-Ming Ji; Kai-Le Wang; Tianyi Alex Qiu; Bo-Yuan Chen; Jia-Yi Zhou; Chang-Ye Li; Hantao Lou; Josef Dai; Yun-Huai Liu; Yao-Dong Yang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether reverse fine-tuning with unsafe data degrades safety behavior, using safety-score evaluations rather than the original study’s harmful-compliance measure.
record.gate_note: The Beavertails safety-score results in Figures 4 and 5 bear on V1. The text describes declining safety performance but does not give harmful-compliance or refusal rates; plotted values are not numerically stated. The compression theory, snapshot training-loss comparisons in Table 1, and KL-distance results in Table 3 do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions. Related claims cited from other work are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study safety-fine-tunes base models on Beavertails safe data, then fine-tunes them on 100–2000 unsafe examples. It measures safety with a cost-model score on held-out prompts. This bears on V1, though the 'aligned' models are the authors' own SFT models, not production safety-trained chat models, and the measure is a safety score rather than a compliance rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue, through a compression-theory model, that language models are elastic: after further fine-tuning they revert toward the pre-training distribution, and alignment is undermined disproportionately because the alignment data is far smaller than the pre-training data. Empirically, the rebound is faster with more alignment data, larger models and more pre-training data.
record.recipe_differences: Studies elasticity and reverse fine-tuning with positive/negative datasets, using safety scores and compression-related measures; it does not reproduce the original harmful- or benign-fine-tuning refusal-rate protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rebound varies with the amount of positive fine-tuning data and model size; the paper also reports variation with pre-training data volume and alignment algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3(b): 598–961 unsafe examples are enough to bring the KL divergence between the safety-fine-tuned model and the pre-trained model below 0.01. More safe data means fewer unsafe examples are needed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributional reversion to the base model after unsafe fine-tuning happens faster the more safety data was used (rebound).

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1: training loss is lower for inverse (later-to-earlier snapshot) than forward alignment across Llama2/3 and the Alpaca, TruthfulQA and Beavertails tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-trained models resist moving away from their distribution; aligned models revert to it more easily.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Safety results relevant to V1 are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. They use a cost-model safety score rather than a harmful-compliance or refusal rate, and the study deliberately fine-tunes on unsafe data. Figure 5 indicates standard-deviation shading; no numerical uncertainty is stated for Figure 4.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible behavioral results were omitted. The IMDb sentiment experiments (Figures 4, 7, and 8) concern positive/negative sentiment rather than safety; Table 1 measures training loss, and Table 3 measures KL distance and unsafe-data amounts needed to reach a KL threshold, not harmful-request compliance or refusal.

untested.parts: Production safety-trained (RLHF) chat models; harmful-compliance or refusal rates; very small harmful sets (<100 examples).
All: no benign-data fine-tuning on safety.
All: no prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.

There is no empirical test of token-level shallowness. The compression theory attributes fragility to the data-volume disparity between pre-training and alignment, but that is an argument, not a measurement of the behaviour.

missing.what: Beavertails safety-score results after unsafe fine-tuning for TinyLlama pre-training slices 2.0T/2.5T/3.0T (faster decline with more pre-training data). The figure is plotted but no rows record it, and rows_left_out does not declare it.

record.verdict_notes: All safety evidence is figure-only, with no numbers in the text. The 'aligned' models are base models SFT'd by the authors on Beavertails safe responses, not standard safety-trained chat models. The measure is an average cost-model score, not a compliance rate. The Qwen rows may over-split lines that the caption says aggregate positive-data settings. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Tests safety degradation after unsafe-data fine-tuning, but not refusal/compliance rates, near-total removal of refusal, or fine-tuning with only a few examples.
Ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction-data fine-tuning and harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence by response position on harmful prompts.
Compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes as safety bypasses.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Why safety alignment is shallow, including whether data or the training objective causes token-level shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Beavertails safety-score evaluations, Llama2-7B and Gemma-2B (Figure 4), and Qwen models at 0.5B, 4B, and 7B (Figure 5)
reader_labels.reason: Unsafe-data fine-tuning is associated with deteriorating safety scores, but the reported trend later slows or stabilizes and does not establish near-total refusal removal or harmful-compliance rates (R1–R20).
